title: The "Player-Coach" Role is Becoming Increasingly Harder
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: An engineering-leadership writer argues that AI coding tools are making the increasingly common "player-coach" role — engineers who both lead teams and stay hands-on technically — harder rather than easier, despite the popular assumption that AI would automate away the "player" half. His evidence is concrete: teams overall are producing 3x more pull requests than in 2024, and teams using AI coding agents produce 6x more, which pushes an ever-growing review burden onto the player-coaches who are ultimately accountable for project success. He identifies a perverse incentive structure at the root of the problem: companies reward engineers for generating large volumes of AI-assisted code (bragging about 50,000 or 100,000 lines a day) while failing to recognize that reviewing and maintaining that code, not producing it, is now the actual bottleneck — meaning less and better code is more valuable than more code. His advice splits by audience: leaders managing player-coaches should resist the story that "AI can just magically do everything for you," actively listen to where review bottlenecks are forming, and give credit for invisible "glue work" like PR review and cross-team communication, not just raw output; player-coaches themselves should build credibility and trust and proactively communicate their impact, since a manager typically sees only about 40% of what they actually do day to day.
points: Teams overall create 3x more pull requests than in 2024, and teams using AI coding agents specifically create 6x more PRs than traditional teams — pushing the review burden disproportionately onto player-coaches, who remain accountable for project success.

Companies increasingly incentivize raw AI-generated code volume (engineers "bragging" about 50k-100k lines a day) while failing to recognize that review and maintenance, not production, is the actual bottleneck — meaning less, better code beats more code.

Leaders should resist the assumption that AI eliminates the need for the "player" half of player-coach roles, and should actively listen to where review bottlenecks are forming rather than dismissing complaints and continuing to incentivize raw output.
Leaders should deliberately credit "glue work" — PR review, proactive cross-team communication, keeping projects on track — not just the people who visibly "create more" with AI assistance.

Player-coaches should treat credibility, trust, and proactive communication of their own impact as core job skills, since a manager typically only sees about 40% of the work a player-coach actually does day to day.
quotes: And teams that use AI coding agents to develop their software create 6x more PRs than traditional teams. And as we know, AI-assisted engineering is the standard way of developing software these days, so most teams are using AI coding agents.

And what can be really problematic is when certain engineers don't review their code correctly, and they just blindly submit "AI-generated slop". And that surprisingly happens quite often, especially with more junior engineers, where that engineer opens a PR full of AI-generated slop, and then it's on the reviewers to find all the issues with it.

Less code and better code is much better, because less code means fewer problems and less maintenance we need to do. With code that's not needed, we are just creating future problems that we don't need.

Company leaders don't understand the bottleneck comes on to reviewing and ensuring the software is built with the right standards. Company leaders think that you can do the "player role" with ease now that AI is here to do all the work and magic.

The first thing is credibility and trust. You need to build both, because without them, your word doesn't have weight, especially with the leadership. Your manager sees about 40% of the work you do on a daily basis, it's your responsibility to communicate the rest to them.
AI makes it easier to create more, but someone still needs to review, prioritize, make good decisions, and ensure everything fits together. And a lot of that responsibility falls on player-coaches.
